## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle components can approach the streaming ceiling on low-churn workloads.

## Cache saturation
At q=0.01, ns/p FALLS from 11.9 at N=4000 (L2-resident, between the L1d spill at N≈910 and L2 spill at N≈58254) to 7.738 at N=65000 (just past L2→DRAM spill), then stays FLAT at 7.8–8.0 through N=4M. No knee at the L2→DRAM spill — the drop is overhead amortization at small N. Death rate raises the floor without changing the N-shape: at q=0.05 the large-N floor is 8.5–9.3 ns/p, at q=0.25 it is 11.9 ns/p, but the curve is flat past N=65000 in all cases.

## Bandwidth
Peak achieved is 9.3 GB/s at N=65000, q=0.01 — 36.9% of the 25.22 GB/s streaming ceiling. The algo is compute/overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. PMC data is absent, so cycle attribution cannot confirm the bottleneck, but flat ns/p at large N and sub-37% utilization point to per-particle compute and branch cost. Bandwidth falls with churn: 9.3 GB/s at q=0.01 drops to 8.4 at q=0.05 and 6.0 at q=0.25, all at large N. The transition is by death rate, not by N.

## Assembly
The compiler vectorized component-wise within one particle, not across particles. `fmul.4s`/`fadd.4s` operate on four position floats of a single particle; `ext.16b` and `mov.s v18[3]` rearrange lanes from scattered scalar loads. The indexed `ld1.s {v17}[1], [x10]` is a single-element gather for one component. The 18 vector-suffixed instructions concentrate in the update loop; the scatter phase (0x100055a80 onward) is entirely scalar `ldrb`/`strb` with `csel` clamping — 19 strb and 12 ldrb doing byte-granular pixel writes. This byte-granular scatter caps bandwidth below ceiling.

## Verdict
Refuted — peak bandwidth is 9.3 GB/s = 36.9% of the 25.22 GB/s ceiling at q=0.01, N=65000, falling to 6.0 GB/s (24%) at q=0.25. Component-wise auto-vectorization within a single particle cannot stream, and the byte-granular scatter stores cap achievable bandwidth regardless of death rate.
